summary: Replatform is the right strategy: fix critical security issues (SQL injection, secrets, auth), replace SQLite with RDS, add production server and logging, and move scheduled jobs to Kubernetes. Readiness is 35/100 due to critical and high findings that must be addressed before containerization.

components.name: inventory-api
components.notes: JSON API plus a health check

components.name: inventory-web-ui
components.notes: server-rendered HTML (Jinja2 templates) with form posts

components.name: inventory-report-job
components.notes: HTTP-triggered job that writes files to local disk; triggered by nightly job via cron (0 2 * * *): http://127.0.0.1:5000/reports/daily

utilization.notes: estimate, not measured: live AWS lookup disabled or unavailable; typical figures for a low-traffic internal Flask app on a 2 vCPU host (options.live_aws is false)

findings.title: SQL built by string concatenation (SQL injection)
findings.evidence: app.py:77 list_items(): "SELECT * FROM items WHERE name LIKE '%" + search + "%'"
findings.recommendation: Use bound parameters for every query and add a regression test with a malicious search string.

findings.title: Secrets hard-coded in source code
findings.recommendation: Rotate the exposed values and load secrets at runtime from AWS Secrets Manager (External Secrets or the Secrets Store CSI driver).

findings.title: Write endpoints without authentication (shared static admin token)
findings.evidence: no auth on POST /items/new (new_item_form), POST /api/items (create_item), POST /api/orders (create_order); item() compares a header to the hard-coded ADMIN_TOKEN
findings.recommendation: Authenticate API clients (OIDC/JWT at the ingress or in the app) and replace the shared admin token with per-client credentials.

findings.title: Service and scheduled job run as root
findings.evidence: ops/legacy-inventory.cron: cron job runs as root; ops/legacy-inventory.service: User=root
findings.recommendation: Run the container as a non-root user with a read-only root filesystem and all capabilities dropped.

findings.title: End-of-life runtime and outdated web framework
findings.evidence: requirements.txt: Flask==2.0.3 (current 3.1), Werkzeug==2.0.3 (current 3.1); system python3 3.9 on Amazon Linux 2023 (end of life 2025-10) runs app.py
findings.recommendation: Build the image on Python 3.12+ with Flask/Werkzeug 3.x, pin versions and scan the image in CI.

findings.title: Internet-facing plain HTTP with an open security group
findings.evidence: ops/nginx.conf: listen 80 without TLS; aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule.http: tcp/80 from 0.0.0.0/0
findings.recommendation: Terminate TLS on an AWS load balancer (ACM certificate) in front of EKS and allow traffic only from the load balancer.

findings.title: Instance hardening gaps (EBS encryption, IMDS)
findings.evidence: aws_instance.legacy: root volume `encrypted` not set (relies on the account default)
findings.recommendation: Encrypt data at rest with KMS (RDS storage encryption, EBS default encryption) and enforce IMDSv2 on worker nodes.

findings.title: Single EC2 instance in one Availability Zone (single point of failure)
findings.evidence: aws_instance.legacy: one instance, no load balancer or Auto Scaling group, single Availability Zone
findings.recommendation: Run at least 2 replicas spread across Availability Zones behind a load balancer, with a PodDisruptionBudget.

findings.title: SQLite database on the instance's local disk
findings.recommendation: Migrate the data to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL (Multi-AZ) so the service becomes stateless and can scale out.

findings.title: Reports written to the local filesystem
findings.recommendation: Write report files to Amazon S3 (or another shared store) instead of the container filesystem.

findings.title: Flask development server used in production
findings.evidence: app.py:149 app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000, debug=False, threaded=True); systemd ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 /opt/legacy-inventory/app/app.py
findings.recommendation: Serve the app with a production WSGI server (gunicorn) inside the container.

findings.title: No backups of the application data
findings.evidence: terraform/main.tf, terraform/outputs.tf, terraform/variables.tf, terraform/versions.tf: no aws_backup_plan, DLM snapshot policy or managed database; data lives only on the instance's EBS root volume
findings.recommendation: Use RDS automated backups with point-in-time recovery sized to the RPO.

findings.title: Configuration hard-coded in source (absolute paths, no environment variables)
findings.evidence: app.py:13 DB_PATH=/opt/legacy-inventory/data/inventory.db, app.py:14 REPORT_DIR=/opt/legacy-inventory/reports, app.py:15 LOG_FILE=/var/log/legacy-inventory/app.log; reads no environment variables
findings.recommendation: Read configuration from environment variables supplied by a ConfigMap and Secrets (12-factor).

findings.title: Logs written to a local file
findings.recommendation: Log structured JSON to stdout and ship it with the cluster log agent (Fluent Bit to CloudWatch Logs).

findings.title: Scheduled job runs from host cron
findings.recommendation: Replace the host cron entry with a Kubernetes CronJob.

findings.title: No health or readiness endpoints for an orchestrator
findings.evidence: app.py:141 GET /status (returns a static string, no DB check); no readiness endpoint
findings.recommendation: Add /healthz (liveness) and /readyz (checks the database) and wire them to Kubernetes probes.

findings.title: Instance over-provisioned for its load
findings.evidence: t3.large (2 vCPU, 8 GiB): CPU avg 4.0%, p95 12.0%, memory 18.0% over 14 days (source: estimate); gp2 root volume (gp3 costs ~20% less)
findings.recommendation: Size pods from measured usage on small Graviton nodes, and use gp3 instead of gp2 storage.

strategy.rationale: Replatform allows us to keep most of the existing Flask code while fixing critical security issues (SQL injection, secrets, auth), replacing SQLite with RDS, adding production server and logging, and moving scheduled jobs to Kubernetes. It is the least invasive option that reaches the container/Kubernetes target and fixes all critical and high findings.
strategy.target: containerized microservice on Amazon EKS + Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL

# Assessment: legacy-inventory

## Executive summary
- **Critical security issues** (SQL injection, hard-coded secrets, unauthenticated writes) must be fixed before any deployment.
- **High reliability risks** (single instance, local SQLite database, no backups) make the current architecture unsuitable for production.
- **Medium operability gaps** (hard-coded config, local logs, host cron) block container/orchestrator adoption.
- **Low cost inefficiencies** (over-provisioned instance, gp2 volume) are easy wins.
- **Readiness score: 35/100** – significant targeted code changes are required to meet container and Kubernetes targets.

## Migration strategy  

| Option   | Fit | Why |
|----------|-----|-----|
| Rehost   | poor | Keeps the monolithic, insecure, single-instance design; does not reach the container/Kubernetes target. |
| Replatform | good | Allows us to keep most of the existing Flask code while fixing critical and high findings (SQL injection, secrets, DB, auth, logging, health checks) and containerizing the app. |
| Refactor | partial | Only needed for the report-generation job if we want to replace the host cron with a dedicated service; not required for the core API. |

**Decision**: **Replatform** – targeted code changes to fix critical/high findings, containerize, and move the data to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL.

## Readiness  
**Score: 35/100**  
Blockers (citing finding ids):
- Critical: LF-01 (SQL injection), LF-02 (hard-coded secrets), LF-03 (unauthenticated writes)
- High: LF-08 (single AZ), LF-09 (SQLite on local disk), LF-12 (no backups), LF-04 (run as root)
- Medium: LF-13 (hard-coded config), LF-14 (local logs), LF-15 (host cron), LF-16 (no probes), LF-11 (development server)

## Next steps
1. Fix LF-01 (SQL injection) and LF-02 (secrets) – use bound parameters and move secrets to environment variables/Secrets Manager.
2. Replace SQLite (LF-09) with Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL and make the app stateless.
3. Add authentication (LF-03) and run the container as a non-root user (LF-04).
4. Refactor configuration (LF-13) to use environment variables, log to stdout (LF-14), add health/readiness endpoints (LF-16) and use gunicorn (LF-11).
5. Replace the host cron job with a Kubernetes CronJob (LF-15) and store reports in Amazon S3 (LF-10).
